title: Single-cell Multiomics
text:
Overview of lesson
Before designing an experiment and collecting samples, it is important to determine which assays will be most beneficial to answering your biological question. Here, we introduce the concept of single-cell multiomics which allows you capture multiple pieces of information (RNA, ATAC, protein expression) within a singular cell. Each modality comes with its own advantages and disadvantages that will determine which analyses you can perform with your data.

title: Single-cell Multiomics
text:
What is single-cell multiomics?
The field of single-cell sequencing has evolved beyond its intial focus on gene expression (RNA) capture. Additional methods have been developed to capture additional information for each cell, including the epigenome (chromatin accessibility), proteome, and more. Experiments that contain more than one modality is what is typically referred to a multiomics experiment.
Two of the most popular protocols that captures all three RNA, ATAC, and protein are ASAP-seq and TEA-seq. This then begs the question, when is it appropriate to use which modality? Kim et. al (2024) summarized the main principles and use cases for each modality. Here, we summarize the key points to serve as a reference for which modality best suits the experimental question or design that you may be using.



Table 1: Summary of common single-cell modalities.












scRNA-seq
scATAC-seq
ADT (surface protein)




Coverage
RNA abundance and splicing events
DNA chromatin accessibility and epigenetic regulation
Surface protein expression


Advantages
• Method of choice for transcriptional heterogeneity• Captures cell-to-cell expression variability
• Short sample prep time and works with few cells• Accessible and cost-effective
• Protein expression is not sparse• Insight into cell communication and signaling• Paired with RNA, better resolves cellular heterogeneity


Limitations
• Low capture efficiency and high dropout making data noisy, sparse, and variable• Incomplete genome coverage, especially in rare cell populations
• Non-specific antibody binding (background counts)• Composition bias from uneven capture efficiency
• Requires known antibodies (challening for non-model)


Applications
• Cell type identification• Cell subpopulation discovery• Gene expression dynamics• Cellular heterogeneity
• Cis/trans regulatory element analysis• Gene regulatory dynamics• Transcription factor activity• Epigenetic changes• Motif analsis
• Gene–protein correlation• Cell signaling pathways• Cell states and cell types

Getting set-up
If you have not already, be sure to download the dataset so that you can access the files used in this analysis. The data can be downloaded from this link

Project organization
When you have large amounts of data, it is easy to lose track of your files and become overwhelmed. We tend to prioritize the analysis and, in the excitement of getting a first look at our data, we often forget to consider how we are going to manage our data and files. This is a common mistake, as data management is often an afterthought when it should be a key part of the workflow from the very beginning. The HMS Data Management Working Group discusses in-depth some aspects to consider beyond the data creation and analysis.
One important aspect of data management is organization. For each experiment you work on and analyze data for, it is considered best practice to get organized by creating a planned storage space. We will do that for our analysis.






Note for Windows OS users



After unzipping, check whether you have a nested sc_multiomics/sc_multiomics folder. If so, move everything from the inner folder up into the outer one, then delete the empty inner folder.




Opening RStudio
We can open the R Project up and see that the provided file structure should look like Figure 3.

Loading your libraries at the top of the script will also allow you to easily keep track of which libraries you are using and to load them all at once in the beginning.

Sample metadata
A great way to keep track of your samples is to create a samples table that contains all the relevant metadata. This can include fields such as sex, batch, date sequenced, and more. Collating all this into one spreadsheet will make it easier to match our dataset with the correct experimental conditions.
Inside the data/ folder, we have provided one such metadata file called samples.tsv. This file contains information about each sample in our dataset. We will first load this in to familiarize ourselves with the data we will be using in the next step.

This table is valuable because it gives us some key information about each sample. For example, we can see that we have multiple sequencing runs from the same patient for many of the HIV negative samples. More consequentially, in the patient column, we see the label pooled for all of the HIV positive samples.
Recall earlier that we discussed that some samples were first tagged with an antibody and then pooled into a singular run. This is a common cost-saving technique used to sequence multiple samples at once. However, in doing so, we must computationally determine which cell comes from which sample by using those hash sequences. This process is called demultiplexing which we will discuss more deeply in the next lesson.

section: Mechanisms of HIV-1 persistence in the gut
text:
Mechanisms of HIV-1 persistence in the gut
Throughout this workshop, we will be utilizing a dataset from Wei et al. (2025). In this experiment, they ran DOGMA-seq on gut tissue from healthy samples and people living with HIV (PLWH) being treated with antiretroviral therapy (ART). As a result, they were able to characterize the transcriptome, epigenome, and proteome of HIV-1 infected cells in contrast to healthy cells.
As a dataset that makes use of hashing (pooled samples), RNA, ATAC, and protein expression, this provides a great learning opportunity to experience how to process each of these modalities (Table 1).



Table 1: Modalities measured in the DOGMA-seq dataset.










Modality
Measures
Used for




Hashtag oligos (HTO)
Sample of origin
Demultiplexing pooled samples, doublet removal


RNA
Gene expression
Clustering, marker genes, cell type annotation


ATAC
Chromatin accessibility
Epigenomic profiles, transcription factor motifs


Antibody-derived tags (ADT)
Surface protein abundance
Validating cell types, protein markers







Key findings
In 2025, Wei et al. published results that showcased which factors promoted HIV-1 persistence in the gut. This study identified BACH2 as a key factor found in HIV-1 persistent T cells in the gut. The authors were able to identify this link across the transcriptome, epigenome, and proteome by using the DOGMA-seq protocol (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Role of BACH2 in HIV-1 persistent T cells of the gut. Image source: Wei et al. (2025)



TODO flush out this section


Samples
This dataset includes 17,642 cells in PLWH and 22,422 cells in HIV− individuals. Each PLWH donor was tagged with oligo-barcoded antibodies, pooled, and then sequenced. From all of these cells, the authors were able to identify 16 distinct cell types in the dataset (Figure 2).






Figure 2: UMAP of cell types identified in the samples collected. Image source: Wei et al. (2025)



To start, we will be using this heterogeneous population of cells to showcase how multiomics datasets are processed. We will first begin with the antibody hashes and protein expression before moving on to the ATAC-seq material.






scRNA-seq



Note that we will not discuss the upstream methods used to process scRNA-seq as we have a separate workshop that details those steps in much more depth.


Lastly, we will pull all three molecular modalities together to run further downstream analyses.

title: Loading the Data and Demultiplexing
text:
Loading the dataset into Seurat
These samples were processed with 10X kits and were therefore processed with their propietary software. Here, we make use of two pipelines cellranger-arc and cellranger multi where the first processes RNA + ATAC and multi takes case of RNA + ADT.
TODO
Therefore, we will have two folders of results that we will eventually merged together into one singular Seurat object.
We will be starting with the ADT protein and RNA expression data for sample PT1.

# Sample of interest
sample <- "PT1"


Load counts matrix
First we will load in the counts matrices from the ADT folder with the Read10X() function. When we investigate the two matrices stored, we can see that we have both the “Gene Expression” (RNA) and “Antibody Capture” (ADT) matrices.

# Load raw counts data
counts <- Read10X(file.path("data", sample, "ADT"))
names(counts)

[1] "Gene Expression"  "Antibody Capture"


Seurat allows you to have Assays() where we can store different matrices for the same cells within a single object. To initialize our Seurat object, let us first use the CreateSeuratObject() function for the RNA expression. Note that we set assay = "RNA", which means that we can use the key “RNA” any time we want to look at the RNA expression over the protein or ATAC values.

# RNA expression matrix
counts_gex <- counts[["Gene Expression"]]

# Create seurat object
seurat <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = counts_gex,
  assay = "RNA",
  project = sample)

seurat

An object of class Seurat 
36601 features across 726385 samples within 1 assay 
Active assay: RNA (36601 features, 0 variable features)
 1 layer present: counts


Now we can see that we have created a Seurat object with 726385 cells and 36601 genes within the assay RNA.


Hashtags

# Protein expression matrix (ADT and HTO)
counts_adt <- counts[["Antibody Capture"]]

We can take a look at all the proteins included in our experiment by looking at the rownames of our counts matrix. In particular we are looking for any “protein” that begins with hashtag. Some runs are comprised of multiple, pooled samples. The way to identify which sample a cell comes from is to use these sequences to demultiplex. The first thing we are going to do here is pull out those antibodies and match them.

# Map of hash to patient
df_hash <- read.csv(file.path("data",
                              sample,
                              "ADT", "hashing_info.txt.gz"),
                    header = FALSE, sep = ":",
                    col.names = c("hash", "patient")) %>%
  # data wrangling
  mutate(hash = str_replace(hash, "H", "h"),
         hash = str_replace(hash, " ", ""))
df_hash

The rownames of the matrix are the names of proteins and hashes, which we can see by looking at the first few proteins in the array:

# View first few protein names
rownames(counts_adt) %>% head()

[1] "GPR56_TotalA"              "ArmenianHamsterIgG_TotalA"
[3] "CD13_TotalA"               "CD57_Recombinant_TotalA"  
[5] "CD272_TotalA"              "CD88_TotalA"              


All the proteins have the string _TotalA appended, so we are going to remove it for easy searching now and in the future. Once we accomplish that, we can search for the hashes in the array by searching for the string hashtag.

# Remove appended _TotalA string from protein names
rownames(counts_adt) <- str_replace_all(rownames(counts_adt), "_TotalA", "")

# Looking for hashes in the dataset
hashes <- rownames(counts_adt)[str_detect(rownames(counts_adt), "hashtag")]
hashes

[1] "hashtag1" "hashtag2" "hashtag3" "hashtag4" "hashtag5" "hashtag6" "hashtag7"
[8] "hashtag8"








More hashes than in dataframe



TODO
In the metadata, we see that there should only be 3 hashes, but we have 8 in our matrix. This is because the sequence for multiple hashes was included in the reference and does not effect the future results.


Now that we have the names for each hash, we can pull those antibody captures out and store it as HTO in our Seurat object with the CreateAssayObject() function.

# Grab counts for just the hashes
counts_hash <- counts_adt[hashes, ]

# Add HTO assay to our seurat object
seurat[["HTO"]] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = counts_hash)
seurat

An object of class Seurat 
36609 features across 726385 samples within 2 assays 
Active assay: RNA (36601 features, 0 variable features)
 1 layer present: counts
 1 other assay present: HTO


To confirm that we added the HTO assay succesfully, we can check that the are 8 Features() in the assay - which should correspond to each of the hashes.

# Name of features in the HTO assay
Features(seurat[["HTO"]])

[1] "hashtag1" "hashtag2" "hashtag3" "hashtag4" "hashtag5" "hashtag6" "hashtag7"
[8] "hashtag8"

Protein expression
Now that we have identified the hashes, we can proceed by adding the protein expression to our Seurat object.

# Protein expression
counts_protein <- counts_adt[!rownames(counts_adt) %in% hashes, ]
seurat[["ADT"]] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = counts_protein)

seurat

An object of class Seurat 
36774 features across 726385 samples within 3 assays 
Active assay: RNA (36601 features, 0 variable features)
 1 layer present: counts

So now we have the RNA, HTO, and ADT assays in our Seurat object. We could also add the ATAC assay, however we will focus on the steps to do so in a future lesson.
Therefore, we can move forward with the next step of demultiplexing.

Filtration
At this point it is quite evident that we have a lot of low quality cells or empty droplets. So to begin
First, we can take a look at the number of total counts associated with each cell to remove cells that have too few counts for the antibody to cleanly assign a sample identity.

ggplot(seurat@meta.data) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = nCount_HTO),
                 fill = "lightblue",
                 bins = 100) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  theme_bw() + NoLegend() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 11)








The black line is drawn at nCount_HTO = 11 to show the threshold we will be using to remove empty droplets. We will additionally remove cells that contain zero RNA expression

# Filter based on HTO counts
seurat <- subset(seurat, nCount_HTO > 11)
seurat <- subset(seurat, nCount_RNA > 0)
seurat

Normalization
NormalizeData(): Normalize antibody counts with normalization.method = "CLR" (Centered Log-Ratio) and margin = 2 (each cell is normalized across its hashtags).
